stage1.topic: First Oil Production and the Long-Run Path of Political Institutions

stage1_5.reason: Path B or data already profiled

top_ideas.title: Staggered DiD: First Oil Production Onset and Democratic Trajectories
top_ideas.research_question: Does the onset of first significant oil production causally redirect a country's democratic trajectory, and does this effect grow or attenuate over the following decades?
top_ideas.method: Callaway-Sant'Anna / Sun-Abraham staggered DiD event study with not-yet-treated and never-treated controls
top_ideas.identification_source: Staggered first-oil production onset driven by geology and capital access timing; not-yet-treated and never-treated countries form credible control groups across cohort-years
data_sources: Polity5 or V-Dem electoral democracy index
top_ideas.pitch: The canonical Haber-Menaldo (2011) finding against the oil curse used TWFE, which is provably biased under heterogeneous staggered treatment effects. This paper re-examines the same question using the Callaway-Sant'Anna estimator on an 83-year, 181-country panel — the cleanest staggered natural experiment in comparative politics. With cohorts ranging from 1930s oil producers to 2010s East African producers, we can estimate how the democratic effect of first oil varies by era, initial regime type, and production intensity.
top_ideas.first_experiment: Identify first year oil_prod32_14 > 0 for each country; categorize into never-treated / early (pre-1960) / mid (1960-1990) / late (post-1990) cohorts; run standard TWFE event study to see raw pattern; implement Callaway-Sant'Anna ATT(g,t) estimates; plot dynamic treatment effects with 10+ pre-treatment periods.

top_ideas.title: Institutional Lock-In from the First-Oil Era: Path Dependence at the Critical Juncture
top_ideas.research_question: Does the regime type at the moment of a country's first oil production permanently alter its long-run political trajectory, even after controlling for subsequent oil revenues?
top_ideas.method: TWFE with interaction between first-oil-era institutional quality (predetermined) and subsequent oil revenue variation; split-sample event study by democratic vs. autocratic first encounter
top_ideas.identification_source: Timing of oil discovery relative to regime formation is determined by geology × political history — both predetermined. Countries where oil preceded regime consolidation vs. where regime preceded oil discovery form quasi-randomly assigned groups
data_sources: Polity5 or V-Dem for first-oil-era institutional quality
top_ideas.pitch: The entire resource curse debate asks whether current oil revenues cause current political outcomes. Nobody has asked whether the institutional quality at the *moment of first oil* — a critical juncture set before wealth materialized — creates a persistent path. Emerging producers like Guyana, Uganda, and Namibia are at this critical juncture today: this paper tells them that how they structure governance before the oil money arrives may matter more than the governance reforms they attempt after.
top_ideas.first_experiment: For each country, extract Polity2/V-Dem score in the 5-year window around first oil production; create binary 'democratic at first oil' dummy (≥6 on Polity); plot raw 40-year post-first-oil democratic trajectories split by this dummy; run TWFE interaction specification: democracy_it = αi + γt + β1(oil_value_it) + β2(oil_value_it × democratic_first_oil_i) + ε.

top_ideas.title: Bartik Oil Price Booms × Predetermined Production Intensity: Windfall Shocks and Democratic Backsliding
top_ideas.research_question: When global oil prices spike, do higher-exposure countries experience larger democratic backsliding — and is the democratizing effect of price busts symmetric with the autocratizing effect of booms?
top_ideas.method: Bartik shift-share DiD: shift = global annual oil price change (exogenous), share = country's predetermined baseline production intensity (geological). TWFE with entity and year FE. Asymmetry test for boom vs. bust.
top_ideas.identification_source: Global oil price changes are exogenous to any individual country's politics; differential exposure via predetermined baseline production share (measured in first 5 years of production) isolates windfall variation from endogenous production decisions
top_ideas.sub_topic: Oil Windfalls, Regime Stability, and Asymmetric Effects
data_sources: V-Dem or Polity for political outcomes
top_ideas.pitch: Most resource curse regressions use oil revenue levels as treatment, conflating endogenous production decisions with exogenous price windfalls. This Bartik design isolates the causal effect of price-induced windfalls — weighted by predetermined geological exposure — and tests whether oil price booms autocratize countries while busts fail to democratize them (a one-way ratchet). If the asymmetry holds, it fundamentally reframes the policy debate: the solution is not price volatility management but institutional design before the first boom.
top_ideas.first_experiment: Compute year-on-year log changes in oil_price_2000 as 'price shocks'; construct baseline_share_i as mean oil_prod32_14 in years 1-5 of production history; run: democracy_it = αi + γt + β(price_shock_t × baseline_share_i) + ε; then split price_shock into positive/negative components and test β_boom = -β_bust; plot heterogeneous effects by initial regime type.
